passage: I'm Vasudha, Hemant's older sister, and I watched him do something odd last Sunday. He spread three months of gig notes across the floor: a price spreadsheet for the tailor, a poster for the bakery, a small website for his tuition class, folding flyers, updating a shop's phone list. Next to each he drew a tick or a question mark. Ticks went beside the spreadsheet and the website. “What will this teach me for college?” he muttered. He crossed out the flyers and the phone list. “Coding first, maybe the poster,” he told me. I don't know whether he was sad to lose the small money, since he went quiet for a while, but then he opened his laptop and messaged the tuition teacher asking for another site to build.

qa.q: Which tasks did Hemant cross out?
qa.a: The flyers and the phone list.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he went quiet after crossing out the small jobs?
qa.a: Some regret at losing the small money, mixed with determination, since he then asked for more coding work.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do to check whether the work fits his goal, and why?
qa.a: He could ask someone who works in coding which skills matter, because it shows whether these jobs are building the right abilities.

qa.q: How might the tuition teacher see Hemant's message?
qa.a: The tuition teacher may see a keen, reliable student who wants to grow his skills, and also gains help with another site.

passage:
September, a Sunday: Ritu had been doing three gigs for three months: typing documents for a lawyer uncle, designing simple websites for two local shops, and babysitting. She sat on the terrace with her cousin Chetan, who was studying engineering. "I'm busy all the time," she said. "But is any of this going somewhere?"

The next Sunday: She made a table. Typing: boring, no new skills. Babysitting: nice, pays okay, but not what she wanted to do later. Websites: she'd learned basic code, fixed bugs at midnight and loved it. "This is the one that feels like the future," she told Chetan.

October, two weeks later: She finished her last typing job and told the lawyer uncle she wouldn't continue. She kept babysitting one evening a week, because the family relied on her. She used the freed hours to take on a third website and to follow a free coding course online.

qa.q: How many gigs was Ritu doing for three months?
qa.a: Three gigs: typing documents, designing simple websites and babysitting.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about the websites?
qa.a: She felt excited and absorbed, loving the work even when fixing bugs at midnight.

qa.q: What else could Ritu do to test her coding path?
qa.a: She could ask Chetan or a teacher which skills matter most for the career she wants, and focus her gigs there.

qa.q: How might the family Ritu babysits for see her decision?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and grateful that she kept one evening a week for them.

grounding: Shows a student asking after three months whether each gig builds skills for a future career, keeping the coding work and dropping the least useful tasks.

passage:
Ojas, you ask whether your weekend jobs are worth it? Let your Tanuja atya tell you what she did at sixteen.

In Kolhapur, I had three small jobs that summer. I sold vegetables for our neighbour in the morning market, I stitched blouses for ladies in our lane, and I helped the pharmacist with his ledger in the evenings.

After three months I was always tired. One night my father asked, "Which of these will still matter when you're twenty-five?"

I sat with the question on the steps. The vegetables, no. The ledger: the numbers made my brain feel alive, and the pharmacist taught me accounts. The stitching I enjoyed but did not want as a life.

So I left the market job. I kept stitching for two regular customers, because they relied on me. And I asked the pharmacist for more accounts work. That is how I became a bookkeeper.

qa.q: What did young Tanuja do in the evenings?
qa.a: She helped the pharmacist with his ledger.

qa.q: How did young Tanuja feel about the ledger work?
qa.a: She felt energised and interested, saying the numbers made her brain feel alive.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shaped her choice?
qa.a: Her father's question about what would matter at twenty-five was the turning point; without it she might have kept all three jobs and stayed exhausted.

qa.q: How might the pharmacist have felt when she asked for more accounts work?
qa.a: The pharmacist probably felt pleased and trusting, glad to teach someone keen to learn.

grounding: An elder recalls asking after three months whether each job built skills for a future career, keeping the useful one and dropping the least useful.
